verdicts.trueWording: Each of us draws his own conclusions about her elusive smile
verdicts.note: Archived 2005 capture of robinhobb.com/rant.html fetched raw. Section 'I should be flattered that readers like my stories enough to want to continue them.' reads: 'To use an analogy, we look at the Mona Lisa and wonder. Each of us draws his own conclusions about her elusive smile. We don't draw eyebrows on her to make her look surprised, or put a balloon caption over her head.' Quote verbatim; analogy, the drawn conclusions and the eyebrows limb all present.

verdicts.trueWording: We have five senses, and in a description of anything, I want to engage as many of them as possible
verdicts.note: lisipieces.com fetched raw (byline 'By Elise Mead', datePublished 2025-10-18). Hobb, quoted in the food section and again verbatim in the Q&A: 'I think it goes back to ‘show don’t tell.’ We have five senses, and in a description of anything, I want to engage as many of them as possible.' Quote verbatim, whole claim supported.

verdicts.trueWording: She maintains geographical consistency, ensuring ingredients match what would actually grow in each region
verdicts.note: Same page, Mead's own prose: 'She maintains geographical consistency, ensuring ingredients match what would actually grow in each region, though she admits to enjoying the occasional imported luxury like ginger root.' Quote verbatim; attribution to Mead paraphrasing Hobb correct (Hobb's own answer says 'I try to keep the menu to what might actually be growing and available in that type of area').

verdicts.trueWording: she wishes she’d determined coinage and monetary values from the start
verdicts.note: Same page, practical-wisdom section: 'When it comes to worldbuilding, she wishes she’d determined coinage and monetary values from the start.' Backed by Hobb's own words in the Q&A: 'Things I wish I’d done? Determine coinage and value of money and stick to it consistently.' Quote verbatim, every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: anchored to a chapter or event rather than page numbers
verdicts.note: Same page: 'Maintaining a glossary where every proper noun goes in alphabetically with a brief explanation, anchored to a chapter or event rather than page numbers.' Hobb's own answer: 'Page numbers won’t work, because they change. Use a chapter or an event to anchor it.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: A tale of three magic wishes works well; an infinite number of wishes is no story at all
verdicts.note: Same page, in Hobb's own interview answer on magic limits: 'It is essential, in my opinion, that magic have limits in a story. A tale of three magic wishes works well; an infinite number of wishes is no story at all.' Quote verbatim; both limbs (three wishes works, infinite is no story) present and attributed to Hobb.

verdicts.trueWording: The geography of Fitz’s world is not a backdrop … full of sight, sound, taste, and cinematic color
verdicts.note: Same page, Mead's worldbuilding section: 'The geography of Fitz’s world is not a backdrop in Hobb’s work. It’s a living entity, full of sight, sound, taste, and cinematic color.' Quote verbatim; the 'not a backdrop' limb is the immediately preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: because at that early point Fitz had no exposure to the world, and so wouldn’t have any notion of what a “iodine smell” would be
verdicts.note: loopingworld.com post (22 September 2025, author Abalieno) fetched raw. The P.S. reads: 'the book is written in first person, but it’s not as much a close perspective as I expected. This early passage at page 21: “I leaned my forehead against his back and felt ill in the brackish iodine smell of the immense water…” I wrote a note there, because at that early point Fitz had no exposure to the world… I was expecting a much more closed perspective there.' Quote verbatim and every other limb (first person, less close than expected, brackish iodine smell, page 21, a perception Fitz could not have had) is supported. Graded PARTIAL only because the blogger never states Fitz's age; he says 'at that early point' and elsewhere 'Fitz, by being just a kid'.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the narrator's age — 'six-year-old' is nowhere on the page; the blogger says only 'at that early point'

verdicts.trueWording: You don’t see melodrama, you don’t see the character screaming in pain, or being in shock
verdicts.note: Same post, paragraph on time jumps and Fitz's voice: 'when something dramatic happens, it’s like there’s no screen. You don’t see melodrama, you don’t see the character screaming in pain, or being in shock.' Quote verbatim; the 'in shock' limb of the claim is the continuation of the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: But I think Fitz voice is actually understated
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'I’d have expected a very strong personality, very strong characterization. But I think Fitz voice is actually understated.' The second limb is supported later in the same paragraph: 'I think this kind of muted internal voice helps to instead bring up the other characters and places. Making the surrounding pieces more lively.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: And it is prose first and foremost, with direct dialogue taking a backseat
verdicts.note: Same post, paragraph beginning 'This was the romantic view': 'For me it was purely the prose… This is a book to enjoy because of how well it is written. And it is prose first and foremost, with direct dialogue taking a backseat.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: some actions don’t seem to have any other consequence … As if the characters shrugged off what happened
verdicts.note: Same post, paragraph beginning 'Even here it’s not all “perfect.”': 'And it’s completely baffling that some actions don’t seem to have any other consequence, without spoiling the plot. The aftermath just appears to be absurd. As if the characters shrugged off what happened, and move on just as usual.' Quote verbatim; the 'final chapters' limb is supported by the same paragraph's frame ('all plot that didn’t happen through most of the book, happens all at once at the end').

verdicts.trueWording: the slow pacing here isn’t a weak point to overcome, it’s where the whole value is
verdicts.note: Same post, the paragraph immediately after the block-quoted reader review of the third book: 'But as the quote above states, the slow pacing here isn’t a weak point to overcome, it’s where the whole value is. You don’t look ahead to anticipate where the story will go, you stay in the present.' Reinforced two paragraphs later: 'To slow down, to be in the present, within the page you’re reading, rather than looking ahead.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: But the novel’s main strength is its narrative voice
verdicts.note: fantasy-hive.co.uk review fetched raw; byline 'By Laura M. Hughes', dated December 8, 2017. Final body paragraph: 'Both the plot and the characters are well-rounded and captivating, as is the setting and worldbuilding. But the novel’s main strength is its narrative voice.' Quote verbatim; the 'not plot or worldbuilding' contrast is the immediately preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: unlike Kvothe, Fitz is brutally honest, and his self-deprecating narrative includes all the damning facts about himself and his own actions
verdicts.note: Same final paragraph: '…brings to the fore a likeable and sympathetic main character who is in many ways the opposite of Rothfuss’s Kvothe. Like Kvothe, Fitz is conscious of telling his own story; unlike Kvothe, Fitz is brutally honest, and his self-deprecating narrative includes all the damning facts about himself and his own actions.' Quote verbatim; the contrast with Rothfuss's Kvothe, the self-deprecating narration and the damning facts about his own actions are all on the page ('rather than flattering him' is the direct sense of 'self-deprecating'/'brutally honest').
